You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Please give a summary of how Covid19 has affected behavior health.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Behavioral Health During the COVID-19 Pandemic
     2	Data from multiple sources suggest that mental health symptoms and substance use have increased
     3	since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. These symptoms include emotional distress and anxiety,
     4	depression, and trauma-related conditions. Substance use refers to the number of individuals using
     5	substances such as alcohol or illicit drugs, and the frequency and quantities of use.
     6	Typically, comprehensive national morbidity and mortality data on mental health conditions,
     7	substance use, associated hospitalizations, and substance-related overdose deaths take months to
     8	compile and report. Comprehensive national data for 2020 are not yet available. Several
     9	organizations, including multiple federal agencies, have used short surveys and rapid data reporting
    10	to monitor mental health symptoms and substance use during the COVID-19 pandemic.
    11	Although the methodological differences between these surveys and perennial surveys make comparisons
    12	between years imperfect, most of the 2020 data suggest an increase in behavioral health morbidity in
    13	the United States over the course of the COVID-19 pandemic.
    14	Mental Health
    15	Data collected from multiple surveys during the COVID-19 pandemic suggest that Americans experienced
    16	increased stress and symptoms of mental health conditions. In a survey conducted in April 2020, the
    17	State Health Access Data Assistance Center (SHADAC)—a program of the Robert Wood Johnson
    18	Foundation—found that over 90% of U.S. adults reported experiencing additional levels of stress
    19	caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. In this context, stress refers to psychological stress, which
    20	occurs when individuals believe that the consequences of a situation outweigh their ability to
    21	adequately cope with it. Reactions to stressors may include fear and concern about the future,
    22	tension and irritability, sadness or depression, or feeling powerless or overwhelmed, among others.
    23	Without adequate coping strategies, stress can have detrimental effects on mental health. Coping
    24	strategies include any behavioral, social, or cognitive techniques used to mitigate the effects of
    25	stress. Coping strategies can be adaptive, meaning they promote better overall functioning (e.g.,
    26	social connections, physical activities, hobbies, good sleep hygiene), or they can be maladaptive,
    27	meaning they are more likely to result in worse overall functioning (e.g., substance use, excessive
    28	screen time, risky behaviors). Although maladaptive coping strategies may reduce stress in the
    29	moment, they may exacerbate problems in the long term.
    30	Many individuals experiencing stress may have adequate coping strategies, meaning that stress is
    31	present but does not impair their daily functioning. For others, stress—and in particular stress
    32	caused by the pandemic—may have detrimental effects on their mental health. A nationally
    33	representative survey conducted by the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF) throughout the pandemic found
    34	that an increasing number of Americans reported that pandemic-related stress was affecting their
    35	mental health. In March 2020, 32% of respondents felt that worry or stress related to coronavirus
    36	had a negative impact on their mental health. In April 2020 that number rose to 45%, and in July
    37	2020, 53% reported that pandemic-related stress was affecting their mental health.
    38	Mental Health Disorders
    39	In some cases, extreme or prolonged stress can lead to mental health disorders. According to data
    40	collected by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), the percentage of Americans
    41	experiencing symptoms of a mental health disorder appears to have increased during the COVID19
    42	pandemic. NCHS—a research agency under the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
    43	(CDC)—partnered with the U.S. Census Bureau on the Household Pulse Survey to monitor the social and
    44	economic effects of the pandemic on American households. The nationally representative survey
    45	collected data on employment status, food security, housing, physical and mental health, access to
    46	health care (including mental health care), and education disruption during the coronavirus
    47	pandemic. NCHS survey questions were designed to obtain information on the frequency of anxiety and
    48	depression symptoms.
    49	Other indicators of psychological distress appear elevated during the first phases of the pandemic.
    50	For example, CDC analysis of national emergency department (ED) visits showed that socioeconomic and
    51	psychosocial-related visits increased during April 2020 (compared with April 2019), while total ED
    52	visits decreased over 40%. Socioeconomic or psychosocial factors were one of a few categories of ED
    53	visits that increased; most of the 200 common diagnostic causes of ED visits decreased during that
    54	same time. Other research suggests that ED visits for mental health conditions may have decreased
    55	during the first few months of the pandemic, to a lesser extent than overall ED visits.
    56	Suicide
    57	Some evidence suggests that suicidal thoughts may have increased during the pandemic. One CDC
    58	analysis found that during the pandemic approximately twice as many U.S. adults reported serious
    59	consideration of suicide in the previous 30 days compared with 2018 (10.7% versus4.3%). Although the
    60	National Suicide Prevention Lifeline did not report increases in call volume, the Disaster Distress
    61	Helpline (part of the Suicide Lifeline) experienced a 335% increase in calls during the first five
    62	months of the pandemic.
    63	The effects of the pandemic on suicide attempts and suicide deaths is unclear, though it appears
    64	that suicide mortality has decreased compared with previous years. An increase in suicidal thoughts
    65	does not necessarily equate to an increase in suicide attempts or suicide deaths.
    66	Research from CDC shows a decrease in emergency department (ED) visits for suicide attempts between
    67	March and October 2020 compared with the same period in 2019, but to a lesser extent than overall ED
    68	visits. Preliminary national suicide mortality data in the United States for 2020 show that suicide
    69	deaths in the United States may have decreased in 2020 compared with the three previous years. In
    70	addition, regional differences may account for changes in suicide mortality. For example, some
    71	individual states and municipalities have reported stable rates in suicide deaths during the
    72	pandemic, whereas others have reported decreased rates. There may be demographic differences in
    73	suicide rates during the pandemic also. For example, CDC reported that in May 2020 ED visits for
    74	suspected suicide attempts began to increase among adolescents, especially girls. Researchers in
    75	Maryland found that suicide mortality rates increased for Black residents from March 2020 to May
    76	2020, while decreasing for White residents over that same time.
    77	Substance Use-Related Overdoses
    78	Comprehensive national data on drug-related overdoses and overdose deaths during the pandemic are
    79	not yet available. Preliminary data from the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) suggest
    80	increases in drug-related overdoses during the first few months of the pandemic. The Overdose
    81	Detection Mapping Application Program (ODMAP), an ONDCP surveillance system
    82	that tracks suspected overdose data nationally in near real-time, reported an increase of 11% in
    83	fatal overdoses and a 19% increase in nonfatal overdoses from March through May 2020 compared with

    86	Notably, ODMAP overdose submissions appeared to be trending upward prior to the onset of the
    87	pandemic, making it difficult to determine the effects of the pandemic and mitigation measures using
    88	these data.
    89	CDC also noted an increase in drug-related overdose deaths in the beginning of the COVID-19
    90	pandemic. Similar to the ODMAP data, the CDC data showed that overdose deaths were already
    91	increasing in the months preceding the pandemic. However, CDC data showed the rate of overdose
    92	deaths accelerating after the pandemic began. In an analysis of provisional CDC mortality data, the
    93	National Institute for Health Care Management found that the rise is particularly notable for deaths
    94	involving synthetic opioids. In addition, the institute reported increases in deaths involving
    95	commonly prescribed opioids and heroin—both of which had been declining in recent years.
    96	 When examining emergency department (ED) visits, CDC found a higher number of drug
    97	overdoses—including opioid overdoses—between March and October 2020 compared with the same period in
    98	2019. Put together, the ODMAP and CDC data suggest that drug-related overdoses and overdose deaths
    99	have increased during the COVID-19 pandemic. Individuals with substance use disorders may be at
   100	higher risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 due to unstable housing situations, high incarceration rates,
   101	or the inability to physically distance themselves. In addition, those with substance use disorders
   102	may be at higher risk for complications of COVID-19 because substance use can often suppress the
   103	immune system or inhibit respiratory functioning.
